title: Configure a Gmail Account in Outlook for Windows
summary: Combining the power of Gmail with Microsoft Outlook for Windows lets you manage all of your emails, calendars, and tasks in one unified, feature-rich workspace. Whether you are using the traditional Classic Outlook or the updated New Outlook on Windows, setting up your Gmail takes only a few minutes.
content:
Why Connect Gmail to Outlook?

Combining the power of Gmail with Microsoft Outlook for Windows lets you manage all of your emails, calendars, and tasks in one unified, feature-rich workspace. Whether you are using the traditional Classic Outlook or the updated New Outlook on Windows, setting up your Gmail takes only a few minutes.

Because modern Outlook applications use secure, browser-based OAuth authentication, you do not need to hunt down IMAP servers or make tricky password overrides anymore—Outlook handle most of the heavy lifting.

Let's look at exactly how to perform this configuration, along with a quick checklist of the prerequisites.

Step 0: Ensure IMAP is Enabled in Gmail (Important Prerequisite)

Outlook needs permission to download your emails. Before you open Outlook, check this Gmail setting:

  • Open Gmail in your web browser and sign in.
  • Click the Gear icon (Settings) in the top right corner and select See all settings.
  • Go to the Forwarding and POP/IMAP tab.
  • Scroll down to IMAP access and make sure Enable IMAP is selected.
  • Click Save Changes at the bottom.

Step 1: Launch Outlook and Start Adding

For Classic Outlook:

  • Click on File in the top-left corner.
  • Select Add Account (located on the Info screen).

For New Outlook for Windows:

  • Click the Gear icon (Settings) in the top-right corner.
  • Choose Accounts on the left menu, then select Your Accounts.
  • Click Add Account.

Step 2: Enter Your Gmail Address

  • In the text box that appears, enter your full Gmail address (e.g., yourname@gmail.com).
  • Click Connect (or Continue on New Outlook).

Step 3: Authorize via the Google Sign-In Prompt

Outlook will now open a secure browser window (or dialog box) powered directly by Google.

  • Re-confirm your Gmail address and click Next.
  • Enter your Gmail password and select Sign in.
  • On the next screen, you will be prompted to grant Microsoft permission to access your emails, calendar, and contacts. Scroll down and click Allow.

Step 4: Finish and Sync

  • A success message will appear in Outlook saying, "Account successfully added."
  • Clear the checkbox for "Set up Outlook Mobile on my phone" if you do not need it, and click Done.
  • Re-launch Outlook to initialize your folders. Outlook will begin synchronizing your Inbox, Sent Mail, and label folders. Please give it a few minutes to download all of your content.
Errors During Login: If classic Outlook refuses to authenticate, you might need to use an "App Password" (if your Microsoft Office suite is highly outdated and doesn't support modern OAuth). Go to Google Account > Security > App Passwords, generate a 16-character code, and use it in place of your standard password in Outlook's Manual Setup (IMAP).
Firewall / Antivirus: Ensure that third-party antivirus software isn't blocking incoming or outgoing ports (IMAP uses 993, SMTP uses 465 or 587).

title: Enable USB Restriction GPO in Windows Server
summary: Restricting unauthorized USB storage devices on your company’s network is a fundamental security practice. Using Group Policy Objects (GPO) in Windows Server, you can globally prevent users from plugging in thumb drives, external hard disks, and other removable media, reducing the risk of data theft and malware infections. Implementing this restriction does not affect vital USB devices like keyboards or mice, as the policy targets the Removable Storage Access class rather than standard human interface devices (HIDs).
content:
Restricting unauthorized USB storage devices on your company’s network is a fundamental security practice. Using Group Policy Objects (GPO) in Windows Server, you can globally prevent users from plugging in thumb drives, external hard disks, and other removable media, reducing the risk of data theft and malware infections. Implementing this restriction does not affect vital USB devices like keyboards or mice, as the policy targets the Removable Storage Access class rather than standard human interface devices (HIDs).

Below is the step-by-step procedure to enforce USB restrictions across your organization’s Active Directory domain.

Step 1: Launch Group Policy Management

  • Opening Administrative Console.

Log in to your Windows Server domain controller with Domain Administrator credentials. Click the Start button, search for Group Policy Management (or type gpmc.msc in the Run prompt), and open the console.

Step 2: Create a New Group Policy Object

  • Policy Creation

In the console tree, navigate to and expand your active directory domain. Locate the target Organizational Unit (OU) containing the computer accounts you wish to restrict (or your workstations container). Right-click on the OU, select Create a GPO in this domain, and Link it here..., and name it something descriptive like Computer-Restrict-USB-Access. Click OK.

Step 3: Edit the GPO

  • Targeting Configuration

Right-click the newly created GPO from the list and choose Edit. This opens the Group Policy Management Editor where you can configure the specific restrictions.

Step 4: Browse to Removable Storage Access

  • Navigating Policies

Within the editor, use the left-hand navigation pane to target the specific policy subfolders: Go to

bash 
Computer Configuration ➔ Policies ➔ Administrative Templates ➔ System ➔ Removable Storage Access.

Step 5: Enforce USB Restriction

  • Policy Setting

In the right-hand panel, find the setting named All Removable Storage classes: Deny all access.

Double-click on it, change its status to Enabled, click Apply, and then click OK.

(Optional alternative: If you want to allow users to read files from USBs but block them from copying files onto a USB, leave that policy as Not Configured and instead enable Removable Disks: Deny write access).

Step 6: Update Policies Across the Network

  • Applying Policy

To instantly push this GPO out rather than waiting for the standard background update interval (which can take up to 90 minutes), open an elevated command prompt on your target computers (or use a remote execution tool) and type:

powershell 
gpupdate /force

Step 7: Verify Configuration

  • Confirmation Check

To test the USB restriction, log onto a target workstation within the linked OU and insert a USB flash drive. Attempt to open it in File Explorer. You should see a dialog box saying, "Location is not available. Drive is not accessible. Access is denied."

You can also verify GPO enforcement by running gpresult /h report.html in the command prompt to inspect applied computer policies.

title: Install Active Directory on Ubuntu Server
summary: Deploying an Active Directory Domain Controller (AD DC) on Ubuntu Server is entirely possible without Windows Server, thanks to the power of Samba4. Samba4 mimics a Windows Server Active Directory environment, allowing you to centrally manage users, computers, group policies, and DNS.
content:
Deploying an Active Directory Domain Controller (AD DC) on Ubuntu Server is entirely possible without Windows Server, thanks to the power of Samba4. Samba4 mimics a Windows Server Active Directory environment, allowing you to centrally manage users, computers, group policies, and DNS.

Setting this up requires configuring static networking, installing the proper backend tools, and provisioning the domain through Samba’s deployment suite.

Step 1: Update and Configure Server Hostname

Ensure your Ubuntu Server has a static IP. Once configured, establish a Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) for the server. Set your hostname (e.g., dc1) and map it to your local IP address:

shell 
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname dc1

Edit your /etc/hosts file and map your static IP (e.g., 192.168.1.10) to your intended FQDN and short hostname:

shell 
# /etc/hosts
192.168.1.10 dc1.corp.example.com dc1

Run system updates to ensure your repository is current:

shell 
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

Step 2: Install Samba and Active Directory Packages

Because Linux lacks native Active Directory features, install Samba along with Kerberos client utilities and standard network backend interfaces. During this installation, you will be prompted to enter your default Kerberos realm—enter it in ALL CAPS (e.g., CORP.EXAMPLE.COM).

shell 
sudo apt install samba krb5-user krb5-config winbind libpam-winbind libnss-winbind libpam-krb5 libpam-ccreds -y

Step 3: Remove Default Configurations

Before provisioning Samba as an AD DC, remove or backup the default smb.conf. This step is critical because the provisioning tool requires a clean slate to build a directory from scratch:

shell 
sudo systemctl stop smbd nmbd winbind
sudo systemctl disable smbd nmbd winbind
sudo mv /etc/samba/smb.conf /etc/samba/smb.conf.original

Step 4: Provision the Samba Active Directory Domain Controller

Provision the AD DC using the samba-tool utility. Using the --interactive flag will guide you through domain naming, DNS backend choice, and password generation:

shell 
sudo samba-tool domain provision --use-rfc2307 --interactive
Quick reference input defaults:
  • Realm: CORP.EXAMPLE.COM (Ensure this is in UPPERCASE)
  • Domain: CORP
  • Server Role: dc
  • DNS Backend: SAMBA_INTERNAL
  • DNS Forwarder IP: 8.8.8.8 (or your internal router IP)
  • Administrator Password: Keep it complex to meet standard AD requirements.

Step 5: Link generated Kerberos Configuration

The provisioning process generates an active Kerberos server file. Link it over Ubuntu's system-wide authentication directory:

javascript 
sudo cp /var/lib/samba/private/krb5.conf /etc/krb5.conf

Step 6: Unmask & Enable the AD DC Service

With Windows AD emulated services ready to start, enable and launch the specialized Samba AD Domain Controller daemon:

shell 
sudo systemctl unmask samba-ad-dc
sudo systemctl enable samba-ad-dc --now

Verify it is running:

shell 
sudo systemctl status samba-ad-dc

Step 7: Configure DNS Resolvers

Disable systemd-resolved to prevent local DNS override conflicts, and point your network configurations to query local Samba DNS:

shell 
sudo systemctl disable --now systemd-resolved
sudo rm /etc/resolv.conf

Write a new static resolv.conf pointing to the loopback IP:

javascript 
nameserver 127.0.0.1
search corp.example.com

Step 8: Perform Directory Audits

Test that DNS, domain levels, and authenticate with Kerberos are performing optimally:

shell 
# Verify domain functional level
sudo samba-tool domain level show

# Authenticate Kerberos tickets
kinit administrator@CORP.EXAMPLE.COM

# List Active Tickets
klist

title: Configure Active Directory in Windows Server 2025
summary: Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the central authority for identity, authentication, and security policies in a Windows environment. In Windows Server 2025, establishing a Domain Controller remains a strict two-phase process: first, installing the AD DS server role, and second, promoting the server to act as a Domain Controller.
content:
Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the central authority for identity, authentication, and security policies in a Windows environment. In Windows Server 2025, establishing a Domain Controller remains a strict two-phase process: first, installing the AD DS server role, and second, promoting the server to act as a Domain Controller.

Before you begin, ensure your server is prepared. You must assign a static IP address, set a permanent hostname (as changing it post-deployment can severely disrupt directory operations), and log in with local administrative privileges.

1.Open the Add Roles and Features Wizard

Launch Server Manager and click Add roles and features directly from the main dashboard. Click Next on the introductory screen.

2.Select the Installation Type

Choose Role-based or feature-based installation, click Next, and select your target server from the local server pool.

3.Add Active Directory Domain Services:

In the Server Roles list, check the box next to Active Directory Domain Services. A prompt will appear asking to add features that are required for AD DS; click Add Features to include the necessary management tools, then click Next through the remaining screens and hit Install.

4.Initiate Domain Controller Promotion

Once the initial role installation finishes successfully, click the notification flag (the yellow warning triangle) at the top right of Server Manager and select Promote this server to a domain controller.

5.Configure the Deployment Operation

For a brand-new environment, select Add a new forest. In the Root domain name field, enter your desired domain structure (e.g., corp.yourdomain.local) and click Next.

6.Set the DSRM Password

Leave the Forest and Domain functional levels at their Windows Server 2025 defaults. Type and confirm a strong Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) password. You will need this credential exclusively for disaster recovery scenarios.

7.Finalize and Install

Click Next to skip the DNS delegation warning (this is normal for a new forest) and confirm the auto-generated NetBIOS domain name. Review the default file paths for the NTDS database, logs, and SYSVOL. Continue to the Prerequisites Check, and once all checks pass, click Install. The server will automatically reboot to finalize the configuration.

Once the server reboots, the default login screen will route you to the new domain, completing your setup.
